questions.stem: An HR coordinator has been asked to redesign the onboarding experience for new warehouse staff. She has a rough idea (a printed welcome pack) but has not talked it through with anyone yet. Before she spends time building anything, how can she use Claude MOST effectively at this design stage?

options.text: Ask Claude to write the complete welcome pack now, so the team has a finished document to review at the next meeting.
Ask Claude which onboarding format is best for warehouse staff and adopt its recommendation, since it has seen many examples.
Describe the goal and constraints, ask for three different onboarding approaches with pros and cons, then review them with the team.
Ask Claude to compare her welcome-pack idea against industry research and confirm it is the right choice before she starts writing.

questions.explanation: Early in design, changing direction is cheap, so the highest-value use of Claude is widening the option space before committing. Giving Claude the **goal and constraints** (shift patterns, reading levels, who delivers onboarding) and asking for **several distinct approaches with trade-offs** reaches beyond her first idea. Taking the options back to the team keeps the decision with the people who own it.

whyWrong.A: Building the full deliverable before the direction is agreed locks in her first idea. If the team prefers a different format, the effort is wasted.
whyWrong.B: Claude can lay out trade-offs, but it does not know this site's staff, constraints or culture. Adopting its pick without team input hands the decision to the tool.
whyWrong.D: Asking Claude to confirm an idea she already has invites agreement rather than real alternatives, and any 'industry research' it cites would still need checking.

questions.mindset: At the design stage, ask Claude for options and trade-offs, then let the people who own the work choose.

questions.stem: A facilities manager wants Claude to help him build a room-booking checklist that front-desk staff will use. He plans to start by typing 'make me a room booking checklist' and then keep adjusting it until it 'feels right'. What should he do FIRST to make the build-and-iterate process more efficient?

options.text: Write down what a good result looks like: who uses it, what mistakes it must prevent, and how he will judge success.
Ask Claude to generate as many checklist versions as possible so he can pick the one that feels most complete.
Start the build with the most capable Claude model so that the first draft needs fewer rounds of adjustment.
Ask Claude to rate each draft out of ten so he knows when the checklist is good enough to share.

questions.explanation: Iteration without a target is guesswork. Defining **success criteria up front** (for example, 'a new desk agent can book a room with no double-bookings and finish in two minutes') gives both him and Claude something concrete to aim at and a way to tell when to stop. Criteria that are specific and measurable make every later round of feedback checkable, instead of a matter of feel.

whyWrong.B: Many versions with no criteria just moves the guessing to the selection step. He still has no way to tell which one is actually good.
whyWrong.C: A stronger model cannot hit a target nobody has defined. The missing piece is a clear goal, not more capability.
whyWrong.D: A self-assigned score is not evidence. Only real users trying the checklist against agreed criteria show whether it works.

questions.mindset: Define 'good' before you build, so every iteration has a target.

questions.stem: A finance analyst set up a Claude Project that answers colleagues' questions about the travel-expense policy, with the policy PDF as knowledge. She tested it with the three questions she used while writing the instructions, and all three answers were correct. She plans to share it with the 40-person sales team on Monday. What is the MOST appropriate next step before sharing?

options.text: Share it as planned, since three correct answers show the instructions are working and users can report problems later.
Ask Claude inside the Project to review its own written instructions and confirm that it will handle every type of expense question.
Add more of the policy as extra knowledge files so the Project has more material to draw answers from.
Test it with a wider set of real expense questions, including tricky edge cases, and check each answer against the policy.

questions.explanation: Questions used while building are the easiest possible test, because the setup was tuned to them. Before 40 people rely on it, she should test with **realistic and awkward cases** (mixed currencies, client entertainment, missing receipts) drawn from real past queries, and check each answer against the policy text. A test set should mirror the real distribution of questions and include edge cases; that shows where the instructions or knowledge need fixing while it is still cheap.

whyWrong.A: Three hand-picked questions are not evidence it works on what sales staff will actually ask. Waiting for users to find errors means wrong reimbursement advice reaches people first.
whyWrong.B: Claude cannot reliably predict its own failures, and a self-review is no substitute for running real cases and checking the results.
whyWrong.C: She has not found any gap yet that more material would fix. Adding files without testing just changes the setup without evidence.

questions.mindset: A prototype is only as proven as the hardest realistic case you tested it on.

questions.stem: A communications officer is refining a Claude-built interactive newsletter planner. After user feedback she asked Claude, in one message, to change the layout, rename four fields, add a word counter and rewrite the help text. Now users say the planner 'feels worse', but nobody can say why. What is the BEST way to continue iterating?

options.text: Ask Claude to regenerate the planner from scratch using the feedback so far, so it starts from a clean design.
Go back to the last version users liked, then reintroduce the changes one or two at a time, checking with users.
Ask Claude to explain which of the four simultaneous changes caused users to feel that the planner got worse.
Keep the current version as is and add a short feedback survey inside the planner so users can explain the problem.

questions.explanation: Bundling four changes at once made it impossible to tell which one hurt. Returning to the **known-good version** and reintroducing changes **in small, checked steps** isolates the cause, protects what already worked, and turns a vague 'feels worse' into specific feedback ('the word counter is fine, the layout is not').

whyWrong.A: Regenerating from scratch throws away what users liked and adds new unknowns, so the cause of the problem stays hidden.
whyWrong.C: Claude did not observe the users, so any explanation it gives about their reaction is a guess, not a diagnosis.
whyWrong.D: A survey may help later, but it leaves users on the worse version and still won't separate the effects of four changes made at once.

questions.mindset: Change one thing at a time so you know what fixed or broke it.

questions.stem: A trainer has an Artifact containing a workshop agenda that his manager approved after several rounds of feedback in the conversation. He wants Claude to draft a very different version of the agenda — built around hands-on exercises instead of talks — drawing on all of that conversation context, while the approved version and its conversation stay exactly as they are and easy to return to. What is the simplest way to do this in Claude?

options.text: Copy the approved agenda into a new chat and ask for the exercise-based version there, keeping the old chat open.
Ask Claude in the same message thread to replace the agenda with the exercise-based version and remember the old one.
Edit one of his earlier messages so the conversation branches, and have Claude build the exercise-based version on the new branch, leaving the original branch untouched.
Ask Claude to put both versions into a single long Artifact, one after the other, so they can be compared.

questions.explanation: **Editing an earlier message creates a new branch of the conversation.** The original thread — with the approved Artifact and all of the manager's feedback — remains intact and can be reopened at any time, while the new branch still carries the full conversation context into the hands-on redesign. It is the built-in way to explore a different direction with zero risk to the approved work: no copying, no overwriting, one action.

whyWrong.A: A new chat starts from scratch: the pasted agenda carries none of the conversation context (the manager's feedback and the constraints discussed) that the new draft must draw on, and the alternative ends up disconnected from the original work instead of being a safe branch of it.
whyWrong.B: This overwrites the approved Artifact in the same thread and relies on Claude 'remembering' the old version — exactly the risk he wants to avoid. There is no preserved, guaranteed copy of the approved work to return to.
whyWrong.D: Merging both versions into one Artifact changes the approved document and buries each version in a single file that is harder to read, edit, or share on its own — it does not preserve the approved version as it stands.

questions.mindset: Branch, don't overwrite: explore alternatives on a new conversation branch so approved work and its context stay untouched.

questions.stem: A sales operations lead used Claude to build a prototype that turns a pasted export of weekly pipeline data into a formatted forecast summary. Leadership now wants it to pull data from the CRM automatically every Friday night and email the summary to regional directors. She will hand it to the internal developer team. Which TWO items will be MOST useful to include in her handoff? Choose TWO.

options.text: The prototype itself plus the written requirements: data fields, schedule, recipients and what a correct summary must contain.
Her CRM login details, so the developers can test the connection the same way she would have.
A recommendation on which programming language and hosting service the developer team should use for building the automated version.
Real sample inputs with the expected outputs, including the cases where her prototype got the forecast wrong.
A commitment to leadership that the automated version will be live by next Friday, giving the team a clear deadline.

questions.explanation: Scheduled, unattended integration with a company system is beyond the Associate scope: the exam guide is explicit that Associates escalate more complex or technical implementations to Claude Developers and Architects. Her prototype is still valuable: together with **clear requirements** it is the best possible specification. **Real examples with expected outputs, including failures,** give the developers ready-made test cases and show exactly where the logic needs care.

whyWrong.B: Sharing personal credentials breaks basic security practice. The developers should get properly scoped access through their own approved process.
whyWrong.C: Technical design choices belong to the developers and architects. Her value is in the business requirements, not the stack.
whyWrong.E: Committing a date before the technical team has scoped the work sets up an overpromise to leadership.

questions.mindset: When a build crosses into integrations, hand over the prototype as the spec, with real test cases.

questions.stem: A program manager has a draft design for a new vendor-onboarding process, produced with Claude's help. It looks polished, and she plans to present it to procurement, legal and finance next week. She wants to use Claude to make the design stronger before that meeting, without handing the decision to Claude. Which TWO requests are MOST useful? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to confirm that the design is complete and ready to present, so she can go into the meeting with confidence.
Ask Claude to review the design as a skeptical finance reviewer and as a legal reviewer would, listing their likely objections.
Ask Claude to rewrite the design in more persuasive language so the stakeholders are more likely to approve it.
Ask Claude to replace the design with a fully automated process so the stakeholders see the most efficient option.
Ask Claude to list the assumptions the design depends on and the open questions she should confirm with each stakeholder.

questions.explanation: Two uses of Claude find weak spots before the real reviewers do. **Critiquing from each stakeholder's point of view** (a role-based request) surfaces objections she can prepare for or design around. **Listing hidden assumptions and open questions** turns them into specific things to check with the right people. Both strengthen the design while the stakeholders still make the decision.

whyWrong.A: Asking for confirmation invites reassurance, not scrutiny. A polished draft can still miss a compliance or payment step.
whyWrong.C: More persuasive wording hides weak points rather than fixing them, and it works against an honest review by legal and finance.
whyWrong.D: Jumping to full automation ignores the approvals and checks these stakeholders exist to protect, and it goes beyond what was asked.

questions.mindset: Use Claude to stress-test a design, not to approve it.

questions.stem: A budget officer asked Claude to help design a departmental budget template. The finance team will fill it in every quarter, and it must work in Excel with their existing macros and sharing folders. Claude is offering to build it as an interactive Artifact with sliders and charts. What should she do to get the MOST usable result for this team?

options.text: Ask Claude for the template as a downloadable Excel workbook (.xlsx) she can test in the finance team's setup.
Accept the interactive Artifact, since its charts and sliders will make the budget easier to understand than a spreadsheet.
Ask Claude to put the template in a table in the chat, which the team can then copy into Excel themselves.
Ask Claude to build both an Artifact and a separate written guide explaining how to recreate it in Excel.

questions.explanation: The right format is the one that fits **how the users already work**. Claude can produce a real **Excel workbook (.xlsx)** that drops straight into the team's existing folders and macros, and she can test it with the finance team in their own setup. A clever interactive tool the team cannot use inside Excel solves the wrong problem.

whyWrong.B: The Artifact may look impressive, but it does not fit the team's Excel-based process, so they would need to rebuild it before using it.
whyWrong.C: A table copied out of the chat carries no formulas or formatting and creates manual cleanup work that a real file avoids.
whyWrong.D: Two deliverables and a recreation guide add work for everyone when Claude can produce the needed file format directly.

questions.mindset: Build the prototype in the format the users will actually work in.

questions.stem: A customer-success lead has spent two weeks refining a prompt that drafts renewal-reminder emails in the company's voice, using a style guide and three example emails. Six colleagues now want to use it, and today each one pastes their own slightly different copy of the prompt. What is the BEST way to package the solution so the team gets consistent results?

options.text: Email the final prompt to all six colleagues with a request to use it exactly as written every time.
Ask each colleague to save the prompt in their personal notes and update it whenever the style guide changes.
Have each colleague tell Claude about the style guide at the start of every chat so it can adapt to their preferences.
Create a shared Project holding the instructions, style guide and example emails as knowledge, and keep it updated in one place.

questions.explanation: A recurring task used by several people needs **one shared, maintained setup**. A Project holds the **instructions and the knowledge files** (style guide, examples) together, so everyone starts from the same configuration, and a single update reaches the whole team. That turns a personal prompt into a reusable team solution.

whyWrong.A: Emailed copies drift as people tweak them, and each update to the style guide means re-sending and hoping everyone switches.
whyWrong.B: Personal copies are exactly what is causing the inconsistency today. Six owners means six versions.
whyWrong.C: Re-explaining the style guide every chat is slow and varies by person, so results stay inconsistent.

questions.mindset: A solution several people reuse should live in one shared, maintained place.

questions.stem: A school administrator built an Artifact for parents to request meetings with teachers and ran a test week. Teachers want more fields (subject, urgency, preferred times), while parents say the form is already too long. He asks Claude to summarize all the feedback. What should happen NEXT to move the design forward responsibly?

options.text: Ask Claude to decide which group's feedback matters more, then update the request form to match the decision.
Use Claude's summary to lay out the trade-off and a few options, then agree the direction with teacher and parent representatives.
Add every field the teachers requested, since they handle the meetings directly and need complete information from parents.
Remove every field the parents found long, since a form parents abandon gives teachers no meeting requests at all.

questions.explanation: Claude is useful for **organizing conflicting feedback** into themes and proposing options (for example, optional fields or a short form with a follow-up step). But choosing between groups' needs is a **stakeholder trade-off** that people should own. Bringing the options to representatives of both groups keeps the solution workable for everyone and keeps the decision accountable.

whyWrong.A: Claude can frame the trade-off, but deciding whose needs matter more is a judgment for the people affected and accountable, not the tool.
whyWrong.C: Siding fully with teachers ignores clear evidence that parents will find the form too long, which could reduce use.
whyWrong.D: Siding fully with parents drops information teachers say they need. Both one-sided fixes skip the trade-off conversation.

questions.mindset: Claude organizes the feedback; people decide the trade-offs.

questions.stem: A sales manager asked Claude to build an interactive Artifact that calculates each rep's quarterly commission from tiered rates. It looks professional, and Claude's message says the logic 'handles all tier boundaries correctly'. He plans to show it to the CFO tomorrow as the proposed tool. What is the MOST reliable way to check it before the meeting?

options.text: Ask Claude to walk through its formula line by line and confirm again that each tier boundary is handled correctly.
Switch to a more capable model and ask it to rebuild the calculator, since a stronger model is less likely to make errors.
Run cases whose correct commission he has worked out by hand, including amounts right at each tier boundary, and compare.
Present it as planned but add a note that the tool was built with AI and that results may vary.

questions.explanation: Claude's statement that the logic is correct is not evidence; self-reported confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal. Plausible-looking calculations can still be wrong, especially at the edges. Testing against **known answers**, including values **exactly at and around each tier boundary**, is a direct, independent check. Doing it before a CFO meeting is proportionate to the audience and the money involved.

whyWrong.A: A second explanation from the same source tends to repeat the same reasoning. It is not an independent check of the results.
whyWrong.B: A different model is also not verified. Rebuilding replaces one unchecked calculator with another.
whyWrong.D: A disclaimer does not make wrong numbers right. Showing an untested pay calculator to the CFO risks credibility and pay errors.

questions.mindset: Verify calculations against known answers; a confident claim of correctness is not a test.

questions.stem: A clinic operations manager built an interactive Artifact that helps front-desk staff estimate appointment wait times. While building it he pasted a sample of real appointment records to test the logic. He now wants to share it with front-desk staff at three sites. Which TWO steps should he take BEFORE sharing it? Choose TWO.

options.text: Publish it publicly on the web so staff at all three sites can open it without needing an account.
Ask Claude to add a visible statement that the tool's estimates are accurate so front-desk staff will trust them.
Check that no real patient appointment records remain anywhere inside the Artifact, and replace them with made-up sample data.
Ask Claude whether the wait-time estimates are reliable enough for front-desk staff to quote directly to patients.
Confirm the tool fits the clinic's AI and data policy, and share it only with the staff who need it.

questions.explanation: Artifacts are private to their owner until deliberately shared, so the moment before sharing is the time to check two things. First, **remove the real patient records** used during testing; made-up sample data is enough for a demo and regulated data should be redacted or anonymized before it spreads. Second, confirm that **policy allows this use** and share only with the intended staff, rather than more widely than needed.

whyWrong.A: Public publishing would expose the tool, and any data in it, to anyone with the link. That is far wider than three sites need.
whyWrong.B: Declaring a tool accurate does not make it so, and it encourages staff to rely on estimates nobody has validated.
whyWrong.D: Claude cannot vouch for its own reliability. That has to be shown by comparing estimates with real wait times.

questions.mindset: Before sharing a prototype, clean out real data and check policy; sharing is a deliberate step.

questions.stem: A marketing manager asks Claude to help build an event-planning tool for her team. Her stakeholders have sent a wish list of twelve features, from budget tracking to vendor contracts to automatic social-media posting. She has two weeks before the next event. What is the MOST effective way to approach the build?

options.text: Agree the one or two features that address the team's biggest pain point, build a small working version, test, then extend.
Ask Claude to build all twelve requested features in one large Artifact so every stakeholder sees their request included.
Ask Claude to rank the twelve features by importance and build them in that order, without checking back with the team.
Wait until she can get a developer to build the full system properly, since a partial tool would only confuse the team.

questions.explanation: A **small version that works** beats a big one that is half done. Starting with the features that address the biggest pain point gives the team something useful within the deadline and real feedback to guide the next round. Some items, like automatic posting to external platforms, are integrations an Associate would escalate to Developers or Architects anyway.

whyWrong.B: Twelve features at once is hard to test and likely to be fragile, and some (automatic posting) need integrations beyond a chat-built tool.
whyWrong.C: Claude does not know which pain points matter most to this team. Priorities should be agreed with the stakeholders.
whyWrong.D: Waiting delays any benefit. A small, tested prototype is useful now and becomes a clear spec if a full build is later justified.

questions.mindset: Start small, ship something useful, then iterate on real feedback.

questions.stem: A logistics coordinator is about to pilot a Claude-built Artifact that drafts delivery-exception notices for customers. She has tested it on two typical cases. She wants a stronger test set before the pilot, with little extra effort. Which TWO actions will MOST improve her testing? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to promise that its drafts will follow company tone for every type of exception notice.
Collect a set of real past exception cases from the operations log, covering the most common types.
Rely on the two typical cases already tested, since the pilot itself will reveal any remaining problems.
Ask Claude to suggest unusual or tricky scenarios (such as partial deliveries or address errors) to add as test cases.
Test only the cases most likely to go wrong, since common cases will be handled correctly anyway.

questions.explanation: A good test set mirrors the real distribution of inputs and includes edge cases. **Real, representative cases** from the operations log show how the tool handles what actually happens; **edge cases Claude helps brainstorm** (partial deliveries, address errors, ambiguous inputs) stress it further. She still judges the outputs herself, but the set is far broader than two typical examples.

whyWrong.A: A promise from Claude is not a test result. Only running cases and reviewing the drafts shows how it behaves.
whyWrong.C: Two cases cannot show how the tool handles the variety of real exceptions. Customers would find the gaps first.
whyWrong.E: Skipping common cases means the most frequent customer messages go unchecked. A test set needs both typical and tricky cases.

questions.mindset: Test with real common cases plus deliberate edge cases; Claude can help brainstorm the edge cases.

questions.stem: Over three weeks, a policy analyst has iterated a Claude-assisted grant-application checklist through about a dozen rounds of reviewer feedback. Her director now asks why certain items were added or removed, and one reviewer wants back an item that was cut in week one. Which working practice would have BEST prepared her for this situation?

options.text: Asking Claude at each round to keep a perfect memory of every past decision, so she can ask it later.
Keeping a short change log for each round: what changed, why, and who asked for it, alongside saved versions.
Regenerating the checklist fresh each round from the latest feedback, so the newest version always reflects current thinking.
Restricting the feedback to a single reviewer, so there are fewer decisions that need to be explained later on.

questions.explanation: A simple **change log tied to saved versions** makes iteration explainable and reversible. She can tell the director why each item changed, and recover the week-one item from the relevant version rather than reconstructing it. It is a lightweight habit that keeps the design process accountable to stakeholders.

whyWrong.A: Claude's recall across many sessions is not a dependable record of decisions, and 'perfect memory' is not something it can promise. A written log she controls is.
whyWrong.C: Regenerating from scratch each round discards history, which makes it harder to explain or undo earlier decisions.
whyWrong.D: Restricting reviewers reduces useful input. The real problem is the lack of a record, not the number of reviewers.

questions.mindset: Log what changed and why, so iteration stays explainable and reversible.
